title: XXIV: Conclusion

teacherSummary.text: Witnesses disagree: most saw a scarlet letter in the minister's flesh, but some saw nothing. Chillingworth withers and dies within a year, leaving his fortune to Pearl, who goes abroad and seems to marry happily. Hester returns years later, wears the letter by choice and counsels troubled women. She is buried near Dimmesdale under one tombstone.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Among many morals which press upon us from the poor minister’s miserable experience, we put only this into a sentence:—“Be true! Be…” slowly and put it in my own words: Of the many lessons, the narrator chooses one: "Be true! Be true! Be true!" Next, craft. I notice the triple repetition, like a sermon's final cry. The strongest word is “true”: it names the novel's central demand: honesty about oneself. Then, effect. What moral does the narrator draw from Dimmesdale's story? My answer: The narrator says that if you cannot show the world your worst, you should at least show some sign of it; Dimmesdale's ruin came from hiding, not only from sin.
